chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Sama'ah, from Abu Baseer, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'If a man has children, is it permissible for him to give his wealth to his relatives?' He said, 'It is his wealth; he does with it whatever he wishes until death comes to him. Indeed, the owner of the wealth may do with his wealth whatever he wishes as long as he is alive. If he wishes, he gifts it; and if he wishes, he gives it in charity; and if he wishes, he keeps it until death comes to him. But if he bequeaths it, then there is for him only the third [portion], except that the preference lies in that he does not neglect those he supports, nor harm his heirs. And it has been reported that the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said to a man from the Ansar who had freed his slaves, having no other slaves than them, so the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) faulted him and said: "He left young children begging from the people."'
ai.seo_question: What are the rules regarding an individual's control over their wealth during their lifetime versus after death in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi delineates the transition from absolute discretionary ownership (milkiyah) during life to the regulated distribution of estate upon death, emphasizing the Sunnah of avoiding financial hardship for heirs. The narrative of the Ansari man illustrates the practical application of this principle, where the Prophet (peace be upon him) critiqued the neglect of dependents despite the validity of freeing slaves, highlighting the balance between individual piety and familial responsibility.
